newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians step up anti-government protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians step up anti-government protests.

text.p: Angry Bulgarian protesters blocked main roads to Greece and Turkey and held nationwide strikes and rallies on Thursday, unmoved by an appeal from the ex-communist ruling Socialists for talks to set an election date.
In Bulgaria's second city Plovdiv, vehicles blocked main city centre junctions and taxi drivers set up a blockade on the principal highway running from Sofia to the Turkish border.
City buses in Plovdiv said they would run only in the afternoon, to carry people to the daily opposition rally.
The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions said strikes had more support than on Wednesday. Schools, factories and mines reported stoppages of an hour or longer.
Thursday was the 25th consecutive day of demonstrations calling for immediate elections and an end to rule by the Socialists, who won parliamentary polls in 1994.

President Petar Stoyanov, who warned on Wednesday that Bulgaria could default on its $10 billion foreign debt, met the European Union's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek in Brussels, who told him not to expect any new aid until political stability was restored.
Socialist Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who is trying to form an interim government, warned on Wednesday that "the chaos and power vacuum may threaten civil peace".

At the town of Doupnitsa, south of Sofia, hundreds of protesters have blocked the main road and railway to Greece since Wednesday morning. Working in shifts, they kept up the blockade overnight, burning tyres to keep warm.
"We cannot afford to buy anything, even meat for our children. We can live without it but the children cannot," said protester Mitko Shopov.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) rejected Dobrev's offer to stand down in the next three to five months and hold elections, saying it wanted the vote now.
Outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December after months of criticism of his handling of the economy and the Socialists' defeat in presidential elections.
They have an absolute majority in parliament but the UDF is trying to secure enough Socialist defections to prevent Dobrev from forming a government.

The Socialists' reformist wing has sharply criticised the party's handling of the crisis, but still plans to support a new cabinet. One deputy has left the party, and a second, Fidel Kossev, said on Thursday he would not support a Dobrev cabinet.
In the equally divided opposition, five deputies left the UDF-allied People's Union in a dispute over election lists.
The Socialists' youth wing cancelled plans for a potentially explosive counter-rally on Friday, after Sofia's UDF mayor set limitations on the route.

In the latest sign of impending economic collapse, state gas firm Bulgargas said it was reducing supplies to big industrial clients who had not paid their bills, because it was unable to pay its Russian supplier and was itself receiving less gas. It said domestic clients were not affected.
The lev fell to 1,450-1,480 per dollar on the interbank market at midday. Technicians had to reset banks' software on Tuesday to accept four-figure quotes.
Branches of the State Savings Bank were quiet on Thursday after savers rushed to withdraw deposits on Wednesday to buy dollars or stock up on food.
Troud daily carried a table showing the minimum monthly wage of 5,500 levs was now worth $3.90, and the average wage of 20,000 levs $14.30, while an average pension of 5,665 levs was worth $4.

Referring to economic protests in Albania, once a byword for Balkan backwardness, it compared the figures with an average Albanian wage of 8,000 leks, worth $72, and an average Albanian pension of 3,000 leks, worth $27.
